story: When I was 10, my aunt told me her kids would always be better than me. Who says that to a child? Long story short, her kids never accomplished anything and are always in trouble with the law.
needed: You were never in a race with her children. A grown woman ranking a 10-year-old said everything about her and nothing about you.
prompt: Who were you measured against growing up? Write down three things you've done that no comparison could ever take from you.

story: My dad had been drinking. He bragged about my older sister being valedictorian, then turned to me and said I should study harder because I wasn't as smart as her. I was already an honors student. I cried in the bathroom. My stepmom stood up for me.
needed: Your effort was never invisible just because he refused to look at it. You were already doing well, and you didn't need to become your sister to count.
prompt: What did you achieve that got overlooked next to a sibling? Write the praise you deserved, then name the person who stood up for you.

story: My mother told me that my brother's child will always be her favorite.
needed: Love was never supposed to be ranked out loud. Being told you come second doesn't make you, or your children, any less worth cherishing.
prompt: Has someone made it clear you or your family came second? Write a promise about how you'll make the people you love feel chosen.

story: My stepmom said she treated me badly because of my stepsister. She said she didn't want my stepsister to get jealous. I was only a kid, and I was treated terribly.
needed: You were never the problem that needed managing. A child deserves kindness in her own home, not to be made smaller so someone else feels bigger.
prompt: Where were you made smaller to keep someone else comfortable? Write to the kid you were and tell her what she should have been given.

story: At dinner, my parents called me their "experiment child." They said they knew they treated me differently than my younger brother because they needed to see the difference in reactions.
needed: You were never a test run. You were a whole child from the start, and you deserved the same care as the one who came after you.
prompt: Did you ever feel like the practice round in your family? Write down what the first-born you actually needed and never got.

story: My dad told me I didn't deserve the life I have and that my sister should have my life instead. We are one year no contact now, and I'll never go back.
needed: Your life was never a prize you had to earn from him. It is yours, and protecting it was an act of strength, not cruelty.
prompt: Has someone told you that you didn't deserve what you have? Write a boundary you've set, or want to set, to protect your life.

story: My mother told me, more than once, that when she left us she only cared about and worried for my younger brother. She wasn't bothered about me at all.
needed: You were worth worrying about, even when she didn't. Her lack of concern was a failure in her, not proof that you mattered less.
prompt: When did you feel like nobody was worried about you? Write a note to your younger self telling her you're checking in on her now.

story: My mom looked right at me and said, "If anybody were to ever get drafted, I would prefer that you did over your brother."
needed: Your safety was never the lesser one. Anyone who could say that out loud revealed their own favoritism, not your worth.
prompt: Was there a moment you realized you were ranked below a sibling? Write about the people who would choose to protect you.

story: A family heirloom was always meant for me. When I finally got the family on my side, my mom gave in with, "Yeah, you're family too, I guess." Years later, it still echoes on quiet nights.
needed: There was no "I guess" about it. You belonged to that family fully, and asking for what was meant for you was never greedy.
prompt: When were you made to feel like an afterthought in your own family? Write the sentence you deserved instead, with no "I guess" in it.

story: My mother decided to stop buying me Easter eggs because I was 34 and she "preferred to spend her money on Easter eggs for my child."
needed: Wanting to be thought of by your mom doesn't expire at any age. A small gesture can carry a big message, and losing it is allowed to hurt.
prompt: What small tradition or gesture did you lose that meant more than it looked? Plan one way to give that to yourself this year.

story: On Thanksgiving, my older brother told me he was “forced” to like me when I was a kid.
needed: You were never a chore someone got stuck with. You are someone people choose, and his reluctance never measured how likable you are.
prompt: Who made you feel like you were tolerated instead of wanted? Write down the names of people who choose you on purpose.

story: My father's last words of wisdom to me were that he didn't want me to be a financial burden on my mother, and he didn't want me to come home anymore. My brother was treated like the prodigal son.
needed: You were never a burden to be sent away. You deserved a place to come home to, and it's not your fault he couldn't offer one.
prompt: What did you need to hear from a parent that you never got to hear? Write those last words the way they should have been.

story: When my dad was at his lowest and planning to end his life, he texted my brothers and my mom a "love you, bye." He never sent one to me. He's still here and we're bonding now, but it still hurts.
needed: Being left off that message didn't mean you were loved less. You're allowed to be glad he's here and still grieve what you didn't get.
prompt: Where have you felt left off the list in your family? Write the message you deserved to receive, in your own words.

story: On my first day of high school, my mom told me she hated me, that she wished I'd never been born, and that she loved my sister more. She hugged my sister, said "I love you," and told me to get out of the car.
needed: You were never the reason she was unhappy. That morning you deserved a hug and a "good luck," and wanting one was always right.
prompt: What was a milestone day that someone ruined for you? Rewrite that morning here the way it should have gone.

story: My mother recently said that I am the daughter she never wanted, and that she is the mother I never wanted. I am 55, and that hurt.
needed: It's never too late for words like that to hurt, and never too late to know they were untrue. You were always worth wanting.
prompt: Has a hurtful sentence found you later in life, not just in childhood? Write about how you'd mother yourself at the age you are now.

story: When I was 12, I got locked up for a probation violation. On the phone call, my dad told me, "It's a vacation when you're gone." I've never forgotten how that made me feel.
needed: You were a kid in trouble who needed his dad, not a relief to be rid of. Your absence should have worried him, and you deserved that.
prompt: When did you need someone most and feel like a relief to them instead? Write the words you wish had come through that phone.

story: "Take it back! I don't want it!" When I was born.
needed: You were never an "it," and you were never returnable. From your first breath, you were a person worth keeping.
prompt: Was there a story about your birth that made you feel unwanted? Write a new welcome to the world for the baby you were.

story: My mother abandoned me at 12. She wanted me to go live with my father, but he didn't want me either. After I hung up the phone, she said, "I guess you'll have to stay now." I'm 47, and I think about it every day.
needed: You were never a leftover no one would take. You deserved two parents fighting to keep you, and the fault is theirs, not yours.
prompt: Have you ever felt like no one wanted to claim you? Write to your 12-year-old self and tell her where she truly belongs.

story: My mom told me she wished she had miscarried me instead of the baby she lost before me. Basically, she said no child could have turned out worse than me.
needed: You were never the wrong child to survive. Her grief and anger got pointed at you, but you have every right to be here.
prompt: What's the cruelest comparison someone made about your existence? Write three true things about who you actually turned out to be.

story: When I was 51, my mom told me the worst mistake she ever made in life was having kids. That was six years ago, and I've been no contact ever since. It's very bittersweet.
needed: You were not her mistake. Choosing distance after words like that isn't bitterness; it's you finally treating yourself as someone worth protecting.
prompt: Were you ever called a mistake, in words or in actions? Write about the bittersweet choice you made, or want to make, to protect yourself.

story: My mom used to tell me she wished she had aborted me. She's gone now. I hope she's looking down and seeing how well I'm doing with my kids, how they love me, and how I raised them the way I wish I'd been raised.
needed: Your life was never a favor she did you. You broke the pattern, and the love in your home is proof of who you really are.
prompt: What words about your existence did you have to survive? Write about the parent you became, or the person you are becoming, instead.

story: I was a twin, and my mum didn't know she was having two. She told me I was the one who wasn't supposed to be here. Now I'm a kindergarten teacher, and I make sure every child knows they have a place in this world.
needed: You were never the extra one. You were meant to be here, and the belonging you give those children was yours all along.
prompt: Did anyone make you feel like you weren't supposed to exist? Write about the ways you now make others feel they belong.

story: "I never wanted you. I could have been a doctor, but I was stuck raising you." That's what my mother said to me when I was 44.
needed: You didn't steal her dreams. The choices she made were hers, and you were never the price of her regrets.
prompt: Have you been blamed for someone else's lost dreams? Write your own dream down here, and one step you'll take toward it.

story: "You're unlucky for me." Thanks, Mom.
needed: You were never bad luck. Her hard times weren't caused by you, and you deserved to be seen as a gift, not a curse.
prompt: Were you ever blamed for things going wrong in someone else's life? Write down three good things you brought into the world just by being here.

story: My mother was shot in a home robbery when I was very young. Later she told a relative, "Why should she have a life when I don't?" The relative told me. She called me terrible names too. She's gone now.
needed: Her pain was real, but it was never yours to pay for. You were always allowed to have a full, good life.
prompt: Did someone make you feel guilty for having a life? Write about one thing you're living fully that she said you didn't deserve.

story: I'm always being criticized, especially for my looks. How do people who claim to love you also love pointing out your flaws, then say they're just trying to help? I know I gained weight. I had a child.
needed: Your body was never a family project. It carried a child, and it deserves respect, not running commentary disguised as help.
prompt: Whose "just trying to help" comments about your body still sting? Write a boundary you'd say to them now.

story: I'd had a terrible day and was resting before a family dinner. My uncle asked my dad if I was seeing anyone. My dad said, "She's too fat. Who would want her?" I was so hurt I don't remember driving home.
needed: You were always worth wanting, at any size. Being lovable was never something your body had to earn.
prompt: Were you ever told your body made you unwantable? Write about someone who wanted you, or who you hope will, just as you are.

story: I gained some weight during a really hard time while starting new meds. My grandma posted a photo of us online, and my mom commented asking how far along I was. I wasn't pregnant. I had just gained a little weight.
needed: You were in the middle of healing, and you deserved gentleness, not a joke. Your body was doing its best through a hard season.
prompt: When did a comment about your body come during a time you were already struggling? Write to yourself in that season with kindness.

story: On the day of my sister's prom, my gran turned to me and asked, "Are you jealous of her because she's skinnier than you?" I haven't spoken to her in ten years.
needed: You were never in competition with your sister's body. You deserved to celebrate her day without being made the punchline of it.
prompt: Has someone set you against a sister or friend over looks? Write something you admire about yourself that has nothing to do with your body.

story: I came home from my first year at boarding school having gained some weight. At the pool, my mum rubbed sunscreen on my back and said, in front of the whole town, "You have bigger love handles than I do." I had to look up what that meant. I was 12.
needed: Before that day, you loved your body without thinking about it. That comfort was yours by right, and you can find your way back to it.
prompt: When did you first learn to feel self-conscious in your body? Write to your younger self about how she felt before those words.

story: My grandma gave me diet pills for my 12th birthday.
needed: At 12, you needed to be celebrated, not shrunk. There was never anything about your young body that needed fixing.
prompt: What gift, comment, or lesson taught you that your body needed fixing? Write the birthday card you actually deserved that year.

story: I'm naturally thin. No matter how hard I try, I can't gain weight. At my cousin's wedding, my aunt asked in front of everybody if I was a cancer patient.
needed: Your natural body was never a diagnosis or a public topic. You deserved to enjoy that day without being made a spectacle.
prompt: Has your body been talked about as if something was wrong with it? Write one thing your body does for you that you're grateful for.

story: During the worst of my eating disorder, my grandmother told me she loved me more when I was bigger. I'll never forget or forgive that.
needed: Love that changes with your size isn't the kind you deserve. You were worth loving at every weight, especially when you were fighting to survive.
prompt: When were you struggling and got hurt instead of held? Write what you needed someone to say during your hardest days.

story: I was eating at my baby brother's first birthday party when my uncle made a whole scene about how he "didn't know I actually ate." He's a licensed counselor. I've struggled with disordered eating since middle school.
needed: You're allowed to eat in front of anyone without explaining yourself. He should have known better, and you deserved a safe table.
prompt: Were you ever made to feel watched or judged while eating? Write a permission slip to your younger self to eat freely and in peace.

story: I feel I'm not pretty enough to have a partner or achieve many things. I told my mom, and instead of showing me I might be wrong, she just nodded, which made me feel even worse. Since I was little, I've suffered mockery, harassment and racist insults.
needed: Her silence was not the truth about you. You deserve to be seen as beautiful, and your worth was never waiting on anyone's approval of your face.
prompt: When did someone's silence confirm your worst fear about yourself? Write what you wish they had said instead.

story: When I was 4 or 5, my grandma looked at me and said, "It's such a shame you're not pretty like your cousin." I've never forgotten it.
needed: Nothing about you was ever a shame. A little girl deserves to be delighted in, not compared, and you were always lovely to look at.
prompt: What's the earliest comment about your looks you can remember? Write a new sentence to that little girl that she can keep instead.

story: I was nine months pregnant, about to give birth any day to a 10-pound baby, and swollen from preeclampsia I didn't know I had yet. My mom told me I "needed to run a few laps around the house."
needed: Your body was doing something extraordinary and dangerous. You deserved care and awe in that moment, not a comment about your size.
prompt: When was your body doing something hard and got criticized instead of honored? Honor it here, the way it deserved.

story: After my first child, a family member told me my husband was going to cheat on me because I had let myself go. He didn't cheat.
needed: You didn't let yourself go. You grew and cared for a person, and your worth to the people who love you never depended on your shape.
prompt: What was said about your body after a big life change? Write a thank-you to your body for what it carried you through.

story: Days after I gave birth to our second child, my then-husband told me, "You're different. Your body just doesn't turn me on like it used to." I was freshly postpartum.
needed: Your body had just brought your child into the world. You deserved tenderness in those days, and his words were a failure of love, not a verdict on you.
prompt: When did someone make you feel undesirable at your most vulnerable? Write down who you've become since leaving that voice behind.
